Vedavyāsa
------------------------------------------
Kṛṣṇa द्वैपायन was the son of the sage पराशर and सत्यवती. Since he was कृष्ण or dark in complexion and was born in a द्वीप or an island, he came to be known by this name.
VedavyāsaIt was he who gathered all the mantras of the Veda available during his time and edited them, dividing them into four parts now well-known as Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda and Atharvaveda. Because of this great work he got the appellation ‘Vedavyāsa’ (‘one who divided the वेदस्’). He was known as व्यास also.
Tradition ascribes to him the author-ship of the epic Mahābhārata, the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas or the major पुराणस्, and the eighteen उपपुराणस् or minor पुराणस्.
Boy गणेश, the little god, is said to have been व्यास’s scribe who took down the Mahābhārata as he dictated it.
It was वेदव्यास who begot Dhṛta-rāṣtra, पाण्डु and विदुर by the command of his मोथेर् सत्यवती, on the wives of Vicitravīrya (son of the king Śantanu).
(See NIYOGA.)
He gave divine sight to सञ्जय (charioteer of धृतराष्ट्र) so that he could describe the कुरुक्षेत्र battle to his master.
Vyāsa was in touch with almost all the important persons of the महाभारत period.

Vedāṅgas
(‘limbs or subsidiaries of वेदस्’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस् are difficult to understand mainly due to two reasons: their archaic language and their complicated ritual system.
Consequently, the six वेदाङ्गस् were evolved even from the ancient times to make them intelligible and practicable.
Though the word ‘aṅga’ literally means a limb, in a more technical sense it signifies a subsidiary field of knowledge that helps us to understand the main work. Hence, वेदाङ्गस् are subsidiary sciences that help us to understand the वेदस्.
The six वेदाङ्गस् are: शिक्षा (phonetics); छन्दस् (prosody); व्याकरण (grammar); निरुक्त (etymology); ज्यौतिष (astronomy) and कल्प (religious practice).
See under each title for details.

vedādhyayana
(‘learning and studying the वेदस्’)
------------------------------------------
Since the वेदस् are considered holy scriptures, their study has acquired a religious character.
A student becomes fit to study the वेदस् only after the उपनयन ceremony.
At the time of teaching the वेदस्, the teacher sits facing the east and the student on his right, facing the north.
After आचमन (ceremonial sipping of water) the student requests the teacher and the teacher consents to start the teaching.
Detailed instructions have been given in the works known as शिक्षा (one of the six वेदाङ्गस्) as to the modes of sitting postures, pronouncing methods, movement of hands and head and so on. For instance, shaking of limbs, lengthening the words like in मुसिच् and restlessness have to be avoided.
If the mantras are chanted as per the prescribed methods, they will definitely produce their effect.

vedi
(‘altar’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices need a special kind of platform or altar usually situated in a शाला or sacrificial shed. Such an altar is called वेदि. It is an elevated plot of ground built or prepared according to the dimensions prescribed in the Śrautasūtra works. These dimensions are fixed in proportion to the height of the sacrificer.
Different yāgas need vedis of different shapes.
VEDI FOR THE NIRŪḌHAPAŚUBANDBAThe वेदि is covered with दर्भ grass on which the various vessels and implements are arranged.

Vedānta Darśana
------------------------------------------
Preamble—Sūtras
The system of एदुचतिओन् in ancient India required the students to live in the campus of a forest academy along with the teachers. The teaching imparted was, almost always, in the form of sūtras or aphorisms, followed by explanations and discussions. At a time when committing things to memory was considered supremely important, this method suited admirably.
The sūtra literature is a class by itself. As per the norms set for a sūtra, it should be ‘alpākṣara’ (consisting of minimum number of letters), ‘asandigdha’ (without doubt as regards the meaning), ‘sāravat’ (must contain the essence of the subject) and yet, ‘viśvatomukha’ (reflect all aspects of the same). However, in their anxiety to economise the words, the composers of the sūtra-works seem to have so overdone it that bhāṣyas or explanatory commentaries by later writers became necessary.
The śrauta, the gṛhya and the धर्म sūtras form the earliest bunch of sūtra literature. The darśanas or the philosophical systems which are of a later period, followed this sūtra model since it served their purpose well.
Vedānta Darśana
Out of the six darśanas or systems of philosophy which accept the authority of the वेदस् (the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्), the last two—the Mīmāṁsā and the Vedānta systems—are directly connected with them. Whereas the former tries to reconcile the various Vedic texts that seem to give different directions with regard to the same ritual system, the latter attempts to make out a coherent philosophy of ब्रह्मन् (God, the Absolute) from the apparently conflicting statements in the उपनिषद्स्.
Prasthānatraya
The Vedānta system, as its very name implies, deals with the उपनिषद्स् which are the end-portions (anta = end) of the वेदस् and also contain the essence (anta = core or essence) of the same. The system itself is based on three canonical works: the उपनिषद्स्, the Brahmasūtras (of बादरायण) and the Bhagavadgītā. The उपनिषद्स् are called ‘śruti-prasthāna,’ the Brahmasūtras, ‘nyāya-prasthāna’ and the Bhagavadgītā, ‘smṛti-prasthāna,’ the three together being termed ‘prasthānatraya’. ‘Prasthāna’ means a school of philosophy or religion.
The Upaniṣads
Though a very large number of works going by the name ‘Upaniṣad’ are available in print today, orthodox tradition accepts only a handful of them—twelve to fourteen—as ancient and authoritative. The entire edifice of the Vedānta system of philosophy depends upon these few उपनिषद्स्.
The teachings of these उपनिषद्स् may, broadly speaking, be classified as follows: ब्रह्मन् as the ultimate cause of this world; nature of ब्रह्मन्; evolution of this world and its character; nature of the living beings as individual souls; their relationship with ब्रह्मन्; their involvement in this world as well as their transmigration; the final goal of life; the disciplines that help in reaching that goal; and, the nature of attainment of that final goal.
It is a fact that the उपनिषद्स्, as extant today, do not give a coherent picture of these various subjects discussed in them. Since tradition and orthodoxy deem the entire body of the उपनिषद्स् as one canonical scripture—the Śruti—it became necessary to reinterpret and reorganise their teachings so as to give them a more coherent look. It was exactly this that बादरायण attempted and the result was the Brahmasūtras.
The Brahmasūtras
The work derives its name from the fact that it deals chiefly with ब्रह्मन् (God, the Absolute) as described in the उपनिषद्स्, in all its aspects. It is also known by other names as follows:
The Vedānta-sūtras, since the subject matter is that of Vedānta or the उपनिषद्स्;
The Śārīraka-sūtras, since the आत्मन् living in the śarīra or the body is dealt with in the work;
) The Uttara-mīmāṁsā-sūtras (as opposed to the Pūrva-mīmāṁsā-sūtras) since it does mīmāṁsā or enquiry into the uttara or latter part of the वेदस्;
d) The Bhikṣu-sūtras since it is specially recommended for study by the bhikṣus or the saṁnyāsins.
Bādarāyaṇa, the Author
Nothing is known about बादरायण, the author of this celebrated work. Traditionalists identify him with व्यास, the author of the Mahābhārata and the पुराणस्. The work is generally assigned to the period 500 B. C.—200 B. C. by the Indian and some Western scholars. However, there are other scholars who consider the two to be different and assign बादरायण to the period A.

.
About the Work
The work Brahmasūtras is in four adhyāyas or chapters. Each adhyāya is divided into four pādas or quarters. The pādas comprise adhikaraṇas or topics, each composed of sūtras.
The total number of adhikaraṇas and the sūtras, according to शङ्कर (A.

-820), the earliest commentator, is 191 and 555 respectively. However, variations are seen in this number as also in the readings themselves. Splitting one sūtra into two, fusing two sūtras into one or adding the last word of a sūtra to the beginning of the next are some of the reasons for such variations in the readings. Such alterations in the structure of the sūtras have contributed to divergent interpretations also. Not only that, divergent views have also arisen due to one school considering a particular sūtra as stating the पूर्वपक्ष (the prima facie view, the objection or doubt) and another school accepting the same sūtra as the सिद्धान्त (the theory propounded by the author of the work).
As already stated, each pāda of the various adhyāyas, comprises several adhikaraṇas or topics. An अधिकरण must have five parts connected in a graded manner. They are:
1) viṣaya or topic; 2) viśaya or सṁशय, doubt; 3) पूर्वपक्ष or opponent’s view; 4) सिद्धान्त or established conclusion and 5) saṅgati or connection between the different sections.
The number of sūtras in any अधिकरण depends on the nature of the subject under discussion. Thanks to the ambiguity in the sūtras, the titles and the number of the adhikaraṇas vary from commentator to commentator.
While निम्बार्क (13th cent. A. D.) has the minimum number of adhikaraṇas (151) Madhva (A.

-1317) has the maximum (223).
The purport of the sūtra itself is determined by the commentators as per the principle of षड्विधलिङ्गस् or six characteristic signs. They are: उपक्रम and upasaṁhāra (the beginning and the end), अभ्यास (repetition), apūrvatā (novelty), phala (objective), अर्थवाद (eulogy) and upapatti (logicality).
True to its name, the work Brahma-sūtras deals primarily with ब्रह्मन् as the highest truth, the only independent truth, by realising which, a person transcends transmigratory existence. The one and only authority for the existence of ब्रह्मन् as also for its true nature is the Śruti, the ज्ञानकाण्ड part (section dealing with the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्/ आत्मन्) of the वेदस् comprising the उपनिषद्स्. This knowledge of ब्रह्मन् can never be obtained by लोगिच् and reasoning which depend upon the puny human intellect. Since the intellect depends upon the knowledge gained by the senses and since ब्रह्मन्, the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् that he is, is beyond the ken of the senses, the Śruti as revealed to the ṛṣis is the only source for knowing him.
This takes us to the next point—the various Upaniṣadic statements that form the basis for the philosophy of the Brahma-sūtras. Since some of these statements appeared to contradict one another, बादरायण had to undertake the unenviable task of collating them to weave out a homogeneous philosophy. While doing it, he naturally chose the most ancient of the उपनिषद्स्. Which are those उपनिषद्स्, the statements of which, बादरायण has discussed in these sūtras? There is no direct indication in the sūtras themselves since they are too laconic. For this we have to depend almost entirely on the bhāṣyakāras or the commentators who, fortunately for us, are more or less unanimous in deciphering the same.
In the first 31 adhikaraṇas (as per शङ्कर) the major statements that form the viṣaya or viṣayavākya (subject-matter) are from the following उपनिषद्स्, with the number of such sentences noted against them:
Chāndogya (14), Bṛhadāraṇyaka (5),Kaṭha (4), Taittirīya (2), Muṇḍaka (3), Praśna (1) and Kauṣītaki (2).
Apart from these, sentences taken from the Śvetāśvatara, the Aitareya and the Jābāla उपनिषद्स् have also been discussed.
While analysing the purport of the various passages from the उपनिषद्स्, बादरायण has quoted the opinions of other teachers also. They are: आत्रेय, Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi, Kārṣṇājani, Kāśakṛtsna, जैमिनि and Bādari. Almost all these names appear in the earlier works like the श्रौतसूत्रस् and the गृह्यसूत्रस्. It is likely that some preceded बादरायण and others like जैमिनि might have been his contemporaries. Though he differed from them, he has not criticised their views, probably because they were also Vedāntins of repute, who had accepted the उपनिषद्स् as the primary authority and ब्रह्मन् as the highest truth.
A Brief Synopsis
The contents of the work may now be summarised as follows:
First Chapter
The First chapter comprising 134 sūtras in 39 adhikaraṇas has been called Samanvayādhyāya, since it attempts to harmonise (samanvaya = harmony) the principles dealt with in the various उपनिषद्स्.
The work starts with the famous sūtra athāto brahmajijñāsā (‘Now, therefore, the desire to know ब्रह्मन्’). Since the knowledge or experience of ब्रह्मन् leads to मोक्ष or freedom from transmigration, it is very necessary to have a correct understanding of ब्रह्मन्. Keeping this in view, the treatise deals with the various statements in the well-known उपनिषद्स् concerning ब्रह्मन्. ब्रह्मन् is he from whom this world came into existence, in whom it inheres and to whom it returns at the end of a cycle of च्रेअतिओन्. The only source for the knowledge of this ब्रह्मन् is the Śruti or the उपनिषद्स्.
It is ब्रह्मन् alone who is the ultimate cause of this world and not प्रकृति or प्रधान as the Sāṅkhyas aver, since it is insentient. An insentient cause can never think or will and produce such a perfectly designed universe.
This ब्रह्मन् is ānandamaya, full of bliss. He is transcendent as well as immanent in this world, including the jīvātmas or the individual souls. The being of light that exists in आदित्य or the sun and our own eyes is also ब्रह्मन्. He is also designated as आकाश, प्राण, bhūmā and अक्षर. The being described as ‘aṅguṣṭhamātra-पुरुष’ (the person of the size of the thumb) is also really ब्रह्मन् and not the जीव, or the individual सोउल्. So also does the word आत्मन् refer to him.
Bādarāyaṇa quotes the opinions of Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi and Kāśakṛtsna in the fourth pāda of this chapter. Āśmarathya thinks that the jīvātmas are both different and non-different from ब्रह्मन् (or परमात्मन्) even as the sparks of fire are both identical with and different from fire. Auḍulomi opines that the jīvas are different from ब्रह्मन् in the state of bondage but become one with him in the state of लिबेरतिओन्. Kāśakṛtsna, however, considers the two to be identical, since it is ब्रह्मन् that has become the जीव also.
Though the views of these teachers are stated, बादरायण does not give his own opinion or preference.
The last part of this chapter asserts that ब्रह्मन् is both the उपादानकारण (material cause) and the निमित्तकारण (efficient cause) of this world.
Second Chapter
Designated as Avirodhādhyāya, this chapter with 157 sūtras distributed among 47 adhikaraṇas applies itself to dispel any virodha or contradiction that may confront this philosophy of Vedānta.
Vedānta is not opposed to स्मृति (secondary scriptures like the Bhagavad-gītā and Āpastamba Dharmasūtras) and तर्क (logic and reasoning). The opposition of schools like that of the Sāṅkhya is fallible. There is no contradiction among the various statements in the उपनिषद्स् dealing with subjects like च्रेअतिओन्. This is the burden of the teaching of this chapter.
Out of the several non-Vedāntic systems of philosophy that existed during बादरायण’s time, the Sāṅkhya system was the most powerful. Hence it has been given special attention while refuting the other schools.
One of the important factors discussed here is the relationship between the कारण (the cause) and the कार्य (the effect). The Sāṅkhyan view known as ‘sat-कार्य-वाद’ states that the कार्य or the effect pre-exists (sat = existing) in the कारण or cause. In the process of च्रेअतिओन् it just gets manifested and is not newly produced, since something real can never be produced from the unreal. On the other hand the Vaiśeṣika school accepts the ‘asat-कार्य-वाद,’ according to which the previously non-existent (= असत्) effect is newly produced. In the former case, the effect pre-exists in the upādāna-कारण (the material cause) and in the latter, the निमित्त-कारण (the efficient cause) is constant. बादरायण accepts these views partially and declares, on the basis of the उपनिषद्स्, that ब्रह्मन् is ‘abhinna-निमित्त-upādāna-कारण,’ both the material and the efficient cause of this world. Hence this world is non-different from ब्रह्मन्. The objection that this world consists of insentient objects and hence cannot be the product of the sentient ब्रह्मन् does not hold good, since the Śruti, the highest authority in such matters which are beyond the powers of the ordinary human intellect, declares it to be so.
Brahman has no selfish motive in creating this world, since he is self-contented. There is neither partiality nor cruelty in this च्रेअतिओन् since justice is meted out to the jīvas according to their karmas or deserts. The very purpose of च्रेअतिओन् of this world is to help the jīvas to attain आनन्द or bliss by getting established in ब्रह्मन्, the Bliss-Absolute.
Apart from the Sāṅkhya school, the other schools like those of the Vaiśeṣikas, the Buddhists, the Jainas, the Pāśupatas and the Bhāgavatas like the Pāñcarātras have also been critically examined and dismissed.
Third Chapter
The third chapter is called Sādhanādhyāya and is the longest, with 186 sūtras spread over 67 adhikaraṇas. Though called thus, the topics discussed are diverse. They are: transmigration of the जीव into other bodies; dream-creations of the जीव; its experiencing the deserts of कर्म by the will of ईश्वर or God; various विद्यास् or meditations mentioned in the उपनिषद्स् and clarifications regarding them; collating of a विद्या when described differently in different उपनिषद्स्; know-ledge of the आत्मन् or ब्रह्मन् as independent of karmas or rituals; certain clarifications regarding the rituals and duties prescribed for the various āśramas (stages of life like ब्रह्मचर्य or सṁन्यास) as also prāyaścittas (expiations) and so on.
Fourth Chapter
Known as Phalādhyāya this chapter is the shortest with only 78 sūtras and 38 adhikaraṇas. The main topic discussed is the journey of the जीव after death to ब्रह्मलोक by the ‘arcirādimārga’ or ‘devayāna’, the path of light or of gods.
One who is interested in मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् has to practise śravaṇa (listening to the scriptures describing the nature of आत्मन्/Brahman) and allied disciplines until realisation. The various upāsanās or meditations described in the उपनिषद्स् aid the जीव in the process of attaining मोक्ष. On attaining ब्रह्मज्ञान or knowledge of ब्रह्मन्, sañcita-कर्म (karma accumulated over several lives) gets destroyed. आगामी-कर्म, कर्म done after realisation, is rendered fruitless. The prārabdha-कर्म, the कर्म that has already started this body and is yielding results has to be exhausted only by experiencing it.
The jīvas who have practised severe spiritual disciplines like तपस् (austerity), श्रद्धा (devoted faith) and ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy), as also विद्यास् like meditation on ब्रह्मन् will travel, after death, by the arcirādimārga or the path of light comprising light, day, bright-fortnight and so on, and reach the ब्रह्मलोक from which there is no return. There are divine guides called ‘ātivāhikas’ who take the जीव through the various stations of light to the ब्रह्मलोक.
Anomalies in the descriptions concerning the details of the arcirādimārga have been set right through proper interpretations and arguments.
The work ends with the declaration, anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt, repeated twice for emphasis, (‘There is no return, since the scriptures declare so’.) meaning that the जीव reaching the ब्रह्मलोक will not return to this mundane existence. Descriptions of the nature of the मुक्तपुरुष, the liberated सोउल्, are given at the appropriate places. The views of जैमिनि, Auḍulomi and Bādari in this regard have also been cited.
The Philosophy of Bādarāyaṇa
Bādarāyaṇa wrote the Brahmasūtras to systematise the teachings of the उपनिषद्स् into a coherent philosophy. However, since the sūtras are short and terse, it becomes quite a job to find out what exactly is his own philosophy as revealed through this work. Even so, with the help of the sūtras which seem to be more unambiguous than the others, an attempt may now be made to portray the same.
The one and only pramāṇa (source of knowledge) that बादरायण accepts while expounding the Vedānta system is the Śruti or the वेदस्, especially the Jñānakāṇḍa part of it, viz., the उपनिषद्स्. He considers the words of the वेदस् as नित्य or eternal. लोगिच् and reasoning, which can always be unsettled by superior ones, can never be relied upon in determining the transcendental truths like the ultimate cause of the world. Smṛtis or secondary scriptures like the Manusmṛti and the Mahābhārata including the Bhagavadgītā can also be depended upon insofar as they do not contradict the Śruti.
The Śruti declares ब्रह्मन् as the origin of this universe, the primary, nay, the only truth. In fact, the very definition (janmādyasya yataḥ,

) makes him the uncaused cause, the ground of sustenance and involution of the world. He is both the material and the efficient cause of the world. He needs no external implements or assistance and can transform himself even as milk is transformed into its products.
He evolves himself into आकाश (ether), वायु (air) and other products by willing the same; and, he is associated with every stage of च्रेअतिओन् up to the last.
Since it is ब्रह्मन् that has evolved into this world, this world is non-different from him, even as an unfolded cloth is non-different from the same which was earlier folded.
The activity of च्रेअतिओन् is a līlā or effortless sport for ब्रह्मन्. But, since it is done as per the karmas of the unredeemed jīvas, one should not attribute partiality or cruelty to him, seeing the good and evil that exist here.
As regards the जीव or the individual सोउल्, बादरायण defines him as a ‘jña’ or knower, a being endowed with चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. He has no birth or death. He is eternal and atomic in size. Whether the जीव is an aṁśa (part) of ब्रह्मन् or his आभास (reflection) has not been stated clearly though the views of other Vedāntins like Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi and Kāśakṛtsna have been given.
The relationship between the जीव and ब्रह्मन् has been likened to the snake and its coiled-up state, or light and its source. Thus the question whether they are different or identical has been left unanswered.
By meditation on आत्मन्/Brahman leading to ज्ञान, or experience of the same, the जीव attains लिबेरतिओन्. The Śrutis give equal importance to the performance of कर्म or prescribed actions and त्याग or renunciation of the same, though the performance of duties prescribed for the respective āśramas (stages of life) has been stressed even for the spiritual aspirant. The fruits of the various upāsanās or meditations practised by a जीव accrue to him by the grace of ईश्वर (Brahman as the ruler of the created world).
On attaining the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्, all the sañcita-कर्म (accumulated past कर्म) of the जीव will be destroyed. He will live as long as the prārabdha-कर्म (karma already fructified) lasts. But, the कर्म done after attaining knowledge will not affect him.
The जीव who has reached the acme of meditation while living, will, after death, travel by the arcirādimārga or देवयान (the path of light or of the gods) and reach ब्रह्मलोक from which there is no return to this world. There, he will be one with ब्रह्मन्, non-different from him. The various attributes predicated of ब्रह्मन् get manifested in the liberated जीव. चैतन्य or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् being his essential nature, is of course, always there.
In conclusion it can be affirmed that बादरायण, in these sūtras, teaches a kind of advaita (Brahmādvaita?). He does not admit the existence of either the jīvas or the world as independent of, or different from, ब्रह्मन्. Since he has accepted the उपनिषद्स् as the supreme authority and since the other teachers like Bādari whom he has quoted, also did the same, he has not contradicted them. Both the views—that ब्रह्मन् is निर्विशेष-cinmātra-svarūpa (pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् without any attributes) and saviśeṣa (with attributes)—seem to be acceptable to him. Obviously he has tried to reconcile the various, apparently conflicting, views expressed in the उपनिषद्स् and explain them rather than formulate his own philosophy.
The Commentators and Their Works
The वेदस् have been the foundation of Hindu religion and culture for millennia. The philosophy of Vedānta based on the उपनिषद्स् has held sway over the intelligentsia for centuries. Hence, it is but natural that the Brahmasūtras of बादरायण has attracted the attention of the distinguished scholars over the years, who have enriched the Vedānta literature by their brilliant expositions. All these commentators have evinced great respect for बादरायण and his monumental work. They have tried to critically examine all the other schools that were important during their days and to prove the superiority of Vedānta over them. Of course, they were equally keen to establish their own school of Vedānta also.
Of the several bhāṣyas or commentaries available to us today, that of शङ्कर is the earliest. There might have been quite a few bhāṣyas composed by the earlier writers. It can however be stated with certainty that उपवर्ष, to whom शङ्कर refers in his commentary (

) must have been one such. बोधायन, another commentator, referred to as ‘Vṛttikāra’ by Rāmānuja, is sometimes identified with this उपवर्ष though there is no unanimity regarding it.

ŚAṄKARA
Śaṅkara’s दर्शन or philosophy as revealed in his bhāṣyas on the Bhagavad-गीता, the ten ancient उपनिषद्स् and the Brahmasūtras is now well-known as Advaita Vedānta. The oft-quoted and famous verse ‘brahma satyaṁ jagan मिथ्या jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ’ (‘Brahman alone is real; this world is only an illusory appearance. The जीव is verily ब्रह्मन् and is not different from him.’) gives this philosophy in a nutshell.
Śaṅkara categorises ब्रह्मन् into two aspects: पर-ब्रह्मन् and Apara-ब्रह्मन्. Where the Upaniṣadic statements deny all limiting adjuncts to ब्रह्मन् like name and form, created by अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे of his essential nature, he is पर, the higher, ब्रह्मन्. On the other hand, where these statements describe him as endowed with name, form and several attributes, it is the Apara or the lower ब्रह्मन् that is referred to. It is the latter that is the cause for the च्रेअतिओन् of this world, its sustenance and its dissolution.
Really speaking, ब्रह्मन् does not get transformed into this world. The multiplicity of names and forms is only a ‘vivarta,’ an appearance, due to अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे, even as a snake is perceived in a rope in insufficient light. This he calls as ‘adhyāsa’ or ‘adhyāropa’ (superimposition). Through विद्या or discriminative knowledge, ‘apavāda’ or desuper-imposition takes place, giving the true knowledge of the reality.
Śaṅkara considers the jīvas as चैतन्य or pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, but, circumscribed by the अन्तःकरण (the ‘inner organ’ or मिन्द्). The जीव, though नित्य (eternal), śuddha (pure), बुद्ध (awakened), and mukta (free), appears as kartā (the doer) and bhoktā (the experiencer) due to the limitation imposed by the अन्तःकरण.
The Upaniṣadic sentences like ‘tat tvam asi’ teach the essential identity between the जीव and ब्रह्मन्, as pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, after eliminating their adventitious qualities.
Śaṅkara does accept क्रममुक्ति or gradual लिबेरतिओन् of the जीव after death, by travelling through the देवयान, to ब्रह्मलोक, as described in the Upa-niṣads and the Brahmasūtras. However, he is emphatic about sadyomukti or instant लिबेरतिओन्, here and now, simultaneously with the rising of ज्ञान or knowledge. Such a मुक्ति is also called जीवन्मुक्ति, लिबेरतिओन् even while living.
RĀMĀNUJA
Rāmānuja’s commentary on the Brahmasūtras is known as Śrībhāṣya. Apart from this, he has also composed two more smaller works on the Brahma-sūtras, the Vedāntadīpa and the Vedānta-sāra. The former, being a later work, contains some additional explanations.
Rāmānuja’s Śrībhāṣya is stated to follow in the footsteps of the more detailed Bodhāyanavṛtti as also the works of some earlier Vedāntins like Brahmanandī and Dramiḍācārya whose works are not available now.
Rāmānuja accepts ब्रह्मन् as the highest and independent reality. However ब्रह्मन् includes in himself cit (the sentient beings, the jīvas) and अचित् (the insentient प्रकृति or nature). These two are also real, but under the absolute control of ब्रह्मन्. Brahman—also called ईश्वर by him—includes them, is immanent in then and also transcends them. Hence, Rāmānuja’s system is called ‘Viśiṣṭādvaita,’ advaita or non-duality of ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, but ‘viśiṣṭa’ or qualified by cit and अचित्. It is similar to a tree with branches, leaves and fruits. Though the tree is ‘one,’ it has internal parts, each part being different from the other parts, the tree itself, however, always remaining as one.
To Rāmānuja, ब्रह्मन् is the Supreme Person (sarveśvara) who is the ruler of all. He is antagonistic to all evil. He possesses infinite auspicious qualities. He is omniscient and omnipotent. The च्रेअतिओन्, subsistence and re-absorption of this world proceed from him.
Rāmānuja considers the जीव or the individual सोउल् as the spirit different from the body, atomic in size and endowed with ज्ञान or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् which contracts or expands. He has a free will. And, the jīvas are infinite in number. Some jīvas called ‘nityas’ are ever free. Others who are now ‘baddha’ or bound, can attain मुक्ति through भक्ति and प्रपत्ति (devotion and surrender) and the grace of God. All the liberated jīvas are similar in nature.
Spiritual life starts with the performance of the prescribed karmas in the right spirit leading to the purification of the मिन्द्. Such a pure जीव becomes fit to practise ज्ञान and experience his separateness from the body-मिन्द् complex. However, it is through भक्ति and प्रपत्ति that he ultimately attains ब्रह्मन् through the देवयान and becomes free.
MADHVA
A thorough-going dualist, Madhva has composed 37 works which collectively go by the name Sarvamūla. The short and terse bhāṣya on the Brahmasūtras, the Aṇubhāṣya a brief treatise on the same in verses, Nyāyavivaraṇa and the Anuvyākhyāna are the four works on the sūtraprasthāna. His is a philosophy of realism and a monotheistic theology centering on devotion to विष्णु or नारायण.
According to him ब्रह्मन्, identified with विष्णु (Nārāyaṇa) is the independent reality. प्रकृति or matter, and the jīvas or souls who are atomic and infinite in number, are coeval realities but entirely dependent on him. ब्रह्मन् is essentially knowledge and bliss. Though his infinite personality is beyond our conception, out of grace for us, he can take forms which are neither material nor finite.
Madhva proclaims the theory of पञ्चभेदस् or five eternal differences between ब्रह्मन् and the jīvas, ब्रह्मन् and प्रकृति, jīvas and प्रकृति, जीव and जीव, and various objects of प्रकृति.
He categorises the jīvas into three groups: मुक्तियोग्यस्, nityasaṁsārins and tamoyogyas. The first group is capable of attaining मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्. The second group, being interested only in the crass pleasure of the world and not a whit in moral regeneration or spiritual elevation, eternally goes through the rounds of births and deaths. The third group of jīvas, the damned sinners that they are, degenerates into lower births and suffers in हेल्ल्.
The jīvas get लिबेरतिओन् through भक्ति and the grace of God. In the state of लिबेरतिओन् they are not only freed from suffering but also enjoy positive bliss. Differences among the jīvas, however, persist even in the state of लिबेरतिओन्.
BHĀSKARA
Bhāskara is the trail-blazer for the post-शङ्कर schools of Vedānta which did not agree with शङ्कर’s brand of advaita based on māyāvāda, the theory of the unreality of this world. He is a strict Vedāntin in the sense that he takes his stand based on the उपनिषद्स् and the Brahmasūtras. His commentary on the latter expounds his philosophy.
Bhāskara advocates the acceptance of the direct meaning of all the passages of the उपनिषद्स् without any distinction. He presents a ब्रह्मन् who has innumer-able auspicious attributes, but, without any particular form. He has a twofold power—the bhoktṛśakti (the power of the enjoyer) and the bhogyaśakti (the power of the enjoyed). Using these two powers ब्रह्मन् transforms himself into the acetana or insentient objects and the jīvas or the sentient souls. Though this transformation is real, it does not affect him in any way. The jīvas in their essential nature are one with ब्रह्मन्, but get differentiated from him in the state of bondage due to the upādhis, or limiting adjuncts—the bodies and minds—which are real. These upādhis, though real, are not नित्य or eternal. They are to be considered real since they are actually experienced. But, in the state of लिबेरतिओन्, they become one with ब्रह्मन् even as the rivers flowing into the ocean become one with it.
Bhāskara considers this world as the kāryarūpa or effect of ब्रह्मन् and hence real.
As regards the sādhana, भास्कर recommends performance of scripture-ordained duties without any desire for their fruits, and the practice of meditation on ब्रह्मन् as also the जीव’s oneness with him. Since he does not accept a Personal God, there is no place for divine grace in his system.
NIMBĀRKA
Nimbārka’s द्वैताद्वैत is very similar to the Bhedābheda of भास्कर. However, being a firm believer in ब्रह्मन् with form and attributes and the path of devotion, his philosophy is more akin to that of Rāmānuja.
Nimbārka’s main work is Vedānta-पारिजात-saurabha which is his commentary on the Brahmasūtras. It is rather brief but lucid, since he avoids the dialectical methods or a flowery style.
According to him there are three equally real and co-eternal tattvas or principles: ब्रह्मन्, cit and अचित्. While ब्रह्मन् is the controller or niyantṛ, cit (the sentient being, the जीव or the सोउल्) is the enjoyer, भोक्तृ, and अचित् (the insentient nature, प्रकृति) is the enjoyed, भोग्य.
Acit is of three kinds: prākṛta or what is derived from प्रकृति or primal matter; aprākṛta or what is not derived from प्रकृति, but derived from a non-material substance of which the world of ब्रह्मन् is made and, kāla or time.
They are different from one another in their svarūpa or nature. But the cit and the अचित् are paratantra-tattvas, dependent realities.
Nimbārka adopts the view that the bheda (difference) and the abheda (non-difference) are both equally real. They coexist but do not contradict each other. It is something like the relationship between the sea and its waves or the sun and its rays. Cit and अचित्, the souls and the universe, exist in ब्रह्मन् from all eternity and never get separated from him, whether in the causal state or when manifested.
They retain their individuality even during salvation, or dissolution of the universe.
Brahman is personal, possesses a celestial body, and is full of exquisite beauty and grace. निम्बार्क identifies him with कृष्ण and posits राधा as his शक्ति or consort even as Rāmānuja accepts लक्ष्मी as the consort of विष्णु-नारायण.
Brahman is omniscient, the cause of the origin, sustenance and destruction of the universe. He is all-powerful and yet all-merciful. He is gracious to his devotees and helps them have a direct vision of himself.
The jīvas are atomic and infinite in number. Each of them is a distinctive agent, a jñatṛ (knower), kartṛ (doer) and भोक्तृ (enjoyer) of the karmas he does. They animate the body they live in, even as a small lamp kept in a room lights up the whole room.
There are three destinies for the jīvas—naraka or हेल्ल् for the sinners, स्वर्ग or हेअवेन् for the virtuous and अपवर्ग or release for the enlightened ones. अपवर्ग is attaining the world of ब्रह्मन् from which there is no return.
Constant meditation on ब्रह्मन् as the inmost self of the जीव or the individual सोउल् is the means of attaining ब्रह्मन् in ब्रह्मलोक. There he has brahma-svarūpa-lābha, becomes similar to him in nature, except for the power of च्रेअतिओन्.
The other sādhanas recommended are: scripture-ordained work, knowledge, devotion and surrender to God, as also strict obedience to the spiritual teacher.
VALLABHA
Vallabha’s philosophy is known as शुद्धाद्वैत. He is said to have written two commentaries on the Brahmasūtras, the Bṛhadbhāṣya and the Aṇubhāṣya, of which the former is not available now. The latter is up to the 33rd sūtra of the second pāda of the third adhyāya (

) only. The book was completed by his son Viṭṭhalanātha. Apart from the प्रस्थानत्रय, he holds the Bhāgavata in very high esteem. He wrote a commentary on it also, called Subodhinī, which too remained incomplete.
For वल्लभ, God the Absolute is कृष्ण whom the उपनिषद्स् call ‘Brahman’. He is one without a second and is sat-cit-आनन्द, (being, awareness and bliss). He has three forms: परब्रह्मन्, पुरुषोत्तम or कृष्ण; अन्तर्यामिन्, the indwelling spirit of all the living beings, and Akṣarabrahman which is the object of meditation and the abode of कृष्ण. It is this अक्षर that appears as प्रकृति (insentient nature, the matrix of all created objects) and पुरुष (sentient सोउल्, the जीव), but is beyond both. While पुरुषोत्तम is the highest, अक्षर is an expression of his.
This अक्षर, again, appears in three more forms: kāla (time), कर्म (action) and svabhāva (nature).
Kāla or time is suprasensible and is inferred from its effects. It is all-pervasive and the support of all beings. कर्म or action is also universal. It manifests itself as different actions of different beings. Svabhāva or nature is that which produces परिणाम or change.
God is both saguṇa and nirguṇa (with and without attributes). He cannot be known except through his own grace. Through his māyāśakti, he can become anything at any time. He is both the material and the efficient cause of this world. He creates the world through his own nature and hence the samavāyi-कारण, the inherent cause. Though he exists everywhere in his tripartite nature as being, चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and bliss, their manifestation in the created universe differs. Matter reflects only the being aspect (‘sat’), the souls reflect the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् aspect also (‘cit’) whereas as ब्रह्मन्, he manifests all the three fully.
Though unmanifest and transcendent in his own nature, by creating the world through his will, he becomes manifest and an object of comprehension. Since this world is a manifestation of ब्रह्मन्, it is never destroyed but is only withdrawn into him at his will.
The jīvas or individual souls come out of अक्षर-ब्रह्मन् like sparks from fire. They are eternal parts of ब्रह्मन् and are atomic in size. They are of three classes: puṣṭi, maryādā and pravāha. The first are the chosen ones enjoying the grace of God, and ardently devoted to him. The second study the scriptures, perform the rites prescribed as ordained duties and also cultivate devotion. They attain God in course of time. The last are interested only in the worldly life and hence transmigrate constantly. Some of them, due to satsaṅga or good company, may attain God later.
Vallabha considers भक्ति or devotion as the only means of salvation. By that, the जीव is released from the cycle of birth and death and enjoys the bliss of God in all possible ways.
Vallabha holds that the knower of ब्रह्मन् is absorbed in अक्षर-ब्रह्मन् and not in पुरुषोत्तम. It is only through भक्ति that the latter, the highest aspect, can be attained.
He advocates two forms of भक्ति: maryādā-भक्ति and puṣṭi-भक्ति. The former is formal devotion to be practised as described in the scriptures and has to be cultivated by self-effort. The latter is attained by the grace of God alone, without one’s effort. ‘Puṣṭi’ refers, not to the physical nourishment, but to the spiritual nourishment got by the grace of God. Hence the name ‘Puṣṭi-भक्ति’. Consequently, वल्लभ’s system is also called ‘Puṣṭi-mārga’. Emphasis on the worship of Bālakṛṣṇa, (child कृष्ण) and sevā or service to him, find an important place in the mode of sādhana taught by him.
BALADEVA
Baladeva is an important teacher of the Bengal school of वैष्णविस्म् developed by श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A.

-1533). The philosophy of this school is known as Acintya-bhedābheda. Govindabhāṣya is his commentary on the Brahmasūtras, Siddhāntaratna being another work that expounds this philosophy. This school, though deeply indebted to the द्वैत system of Madhva, also differs from it.
According to this school of thought, ब्रह्मन् the highest reality is कृष्ण, विष्णु or Hari. He is the Personal God possessing infinite auspicious qualities, which are ‘acintya’ or beyond our comprehension. He is ‘nirguṇa’ only in the sense that he is beyond the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्. The scriptures are the only authority to reveal him.
God has three powers: पराशक्ति (higher power), aparāśakti (lower power) and avidyāśakti (nescience-power). Through the first, he becomes the efficient cause, and, through the other two, the material cause. When the latter two powers are manifested in gross forms, the universe of souls and matter arises.
Creation of the world is a spontaneous act of the Lord. However, he does it as per the karmas of the individual souls.
The individual सोउल् is eternal. It is both knowledge and knower, an enjoyer and an active agent, though not independent. It is atomic in size.
Bhakti is the sole and direct cause of salvation. Though ध्यान or upāsanā (meditation) is one form of भक्ति, it is through premābhakti (intense devotion) that God can be realised. Performance of duties purifies the मिन्द्. Study of the scriptures is an aid in the path of sādhana. However, it is ultimately by the grace of God alone that he can be realised and salvation attained. The freed सोउल् resides in the same world as the lord and in his proximity, and attains his nature and attributes. However, it retains its separate identity.
Baladeva does not accept of जीवन्मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् while living in the body here.
The ब्रह्मसूत्र Literature
Being the basic text of Vedānta, both in its metaphysical and in its dialectical aspect, the Brahmasūtras has attracted the attention of a host of elite scholars over the centuries. Apart from the direct bhāṣyas by the great ācāryas, several subcommentaries and glosses over them have enriched the ब्रह्मसूत्र literature. In such literature now available to us, the maximum number of works belong to the Advaita school.
On the Śāṅkarabhāṣya, three ṭīkās or subcommentaries are available in full: Bhāmatī of Vācaspatimiśra (A.
), Nyāyanirṇaya of आनन्दगिरि (A.

) and Ratnaprabhā of रामानन्द (17th century)

Apart from these works mentioned here, there are several other treatises and tracts on the various aspects of Vedānta as interpreted by the numerous schools.
Conclusion
There is no gainsaying the fact that the Vedānta system based chiefly on the Brahmasūtras—which itself is a systematic exposition of the philosophy of the Upaniṣads—has influenced all the important aspects of Hindu religion and culture, including the modern Hindu movements.

Introduction
The word ‘Veda,’ derived from the root vid (‘to know’), indicates a vast body of sacred and esoteric knowledge concerning the eternal spiritual values revealed to the great ones called ṛṣis (men of wisdom, sages) in the depths of their meditation. The Hindu religious tradition has accorded the वेदस् the highest place in its canonical literature. As such, they are revered as the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्.
It is extremely difficult to fix the date of the वेदस्. The dates assigned by the various scholars vary as widely as 25,000 B. C. to 1000 B. C. However the general consensus among most of the Indian scholars is to consider the हरप्प-Mohenjo Daro culture (c. 4000 B. C.) to be a later phase of the Vedic culture. This places the date of the Ṛg-veda, the earliest of the वेदस्, around 10,000 B. C.
For centuries, the वेदस् have been handed down to the posterity by oral tradition. Hence the name Śruti, ‘what is heard’. And, they have been mainly utilized in the performance of yajñas and yāgas (sacrifices), which were the most common form of early Vedic religion. Such utilization of the वेदस् in the sacrificial processes naturally led to its division based upon the convenience of the chief priests conducting the sacrifices.
A compilation of all the hymns used by the hotā-priest to invite the various deities to the sacrifice became the Ṛgveda. All the liturgical parts of the वेदस्, useful to the अध्वर्यु-priest, the chief executor of the sacrificial rites, brought together, formed the Yajurveda. Collection of all the musical chants, especially those associated with the सोम group of sacrifices, and to be sung by the उद्गातृ-priest, the singer, was named as Sāmaveda. The rest, a sort of miscellaneous appendix and addenda, became the Atharvaveda and was assigned to the ब्रह्मा-priest, considered as the supervisor over the whole sacrificial process.
As per the annals of the Hindu orthodoxy, the great sage कृष्ण द्वैपायन व्यास effected this division by collecting all the mantras extant during his time, and editing them into four groups: Ṛk, Yajus, सामन् and अथर्वन्. He taught them to his four chief disciples: पैल (Ṛgveda), वैशम्पायन (Yajurveda), जैमिनि (Sāmaveda) and सुमन्तु (Atharvaveda). This is how these four वेदस् took shape.
The वेदस् are divided in another way too: मन्त्र and ब्राह्मण. Saṁhitā is the name given to the collection of the Mantras. The ब्राह्मण includes in itself two more sections, the Āraṇyaka and the Upaniṣad. If the Mantras comprise the hymns, the ब्राह्मणस् contain liturgies in prose. The आरण्यकस् teach about medi-tations based on symbolical interpretations of the liturgical rites. The उपनिषद्स् may roughly be defined as philosophical treatises dealing with the ultimate problems of life.
Conventionally speaking, it is the Saṁhitā that is indicated by the word Veda. For instance, Ṛgveda means only the Ṛksaṁhitā or the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā. The ब्राह्मणस्, the आरण्यकस् and the उपनिषद्स् of the Ṛgveda have different and independent names and are considered more like its appendages.
These Saṁhitās, in course of time, branched off, leading to the formation of शाखास् or recensions. The origin of these शाखास् probably lies in the fact that each of the principal sages like पैल or वैशम्पायन had several disciples. These disciples or their successors might have done some editing and readjustment of the Vedic mantras to suit the needs of the rites which they had to perform and upon which local culture too might have exerted its influence.
A brief account of the contents of the four वेदस् may now be attempted here.
Ṛgveda Saṁhitā
Of all the four Vedic Saṁhitās, the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā is the oldest and has a pre-eminent place in the Vedic literature. It is a collection of sūktas or hymns revealed to various ṛṣis or sages at different periods of time. Consequently we can notice a variety of styles of language, grammar, ideas as also historical and cultural factors.
Though it is said to have had 21 शाखास्, only five are known to be extant: Śākala, Bāṣkala, आश्वलायन, Śāṅkhā-yana and Māṇḍūkeya. Except for the order of arrangement of the sūktas there do not seem to be any substantial variations among them.
Since ancient days, two methods of dividing this Veda are in vogue. In the first, it is divided into eight aṣṭakas. Each अष्टक is subdivided into vargas, containing mantras. This mode of division has been done obviously with a view to facili-tating memorization, since the number of vargas in each अष्टक and the mantras in each varga is more or less the same. A total of 10,552 mantras are spread over 2,024 vargas, included in the 64 adhyāyas of the eight aṣṭakas.
In the second method, the whole Saṁhitā has been divided into ten maṇḍalas. The maṇḍalas are subdivided into anuvākas, the anuvākas into sūktas and the sūktas into mantras. The number of anuvākas is 85, that of the sūktas 1,028, the total number of mantras being, of course, the same.
The latter method seems to be the more ancient one and has universal approval among the modern Vedic scholars.
There seems to be some method and order in the arrangement of the sūktas into the ten maṇḍalas. The six maṇḍalas (two to seven) contain sūktas revealed to the ṛṣis of the same generic group (vaṁśa). For instance, if the seers of the sūktas in the second मण्डल belong to the lineage of गृत्समद, those in the third belong to the descendants of विश्वामित्र and so on.
The first and the eighth maṇḍalas contain respectively the sūktas of Śatarcins and Pragāthas. The sūktas of the ninth मण्डल are all in praise of a single deity—Soma Pavamāna—and are classified according to their metres. The last, the tenth मण्डल, is a miscellany of sūktas inclined more towards metaphysical subjects.
The topics dealt with in the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā fall roughly into three groups. The first group deals with the deities like अग्नि, इन्द्र, वरुण, and others. The second group is concerned with philosophical speculations like the origin of the universe and the real nature of human beings. The third group deals with several secular subjects like मर्रिअगे, wars of kings, eulogy of generosity and so on.
The Vedic deities are usually enumerated as 33—8 वसुस्, 11 Rudras, 12 Ādityas, इन्द्र and प्रजापति. These deities are assigned to the three regions of earth (pṛthvī), heavens (dyaus) and the intermediary space (antarikṣa). Though they appear like personifications of forces of nature, they are all actually facets of ब्रह्मन्, the Supreme Truth. The मन्त्र in which the well-known statement, ekaṁ sat, viprāḥ bahudhā vadanti [‘Truth is one; sages call It by various names.’] (1.164.46) occurs, is proof enough of this fact. (vide 7.58.2; 10.114.5;

; 2.13.6 also.) However, it may be noted that इन्द्र, अग्नि, वरुण and मित्र have been given the pride of place in the hymns.
Coming to the philosophical speculations of this Veda, we find that it is the origin and repository of almost all the later ideas of Vedānta including ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion), though some of them are in a seed form. This forces us to concede that it is not a book of laudatory hymns only as some try to make it out.
As already pointed out, it teaches eka-devatā-vāda or monotheism and not polytheism, as is often mistakenly assumed. However, advocacy of saguṇopāsanā (worship of God with form and qualities) is predominant.
God creates this world out of Himself (10.8

) and rules over it (10.82.1; 6.19.10; 6.45.20). He is omnipresent (1.13.10), omniscient (6.7.6; 8.25.9) and omnipotent (6.30.1; 2.29.3; 3.59.1). He is ever perfect (6.24.7; 6.11.4). But He is infinitely compassionate (2.34.5) and easily approachable by the devotees (8.32.15). He is our dearest friend (10.80.2) and grants us इम्मोर्तलित्य् (6.45.6; 5.47.7).
As regards the actual process of च्रेअतिओन्, we find two streams of thought, च्रेअतिओन् and evolution, both of which have been found in the later Vedāntic literature.
Though the existence of the सोउल् as an eternal entity is accepted and अमृतत्व or इम्मोर्तलित्य् is prayed for, the life here-and-now is not relegated to the background. Life here and life hereafter have been nicely harmonized.
From the group of sūktas dealing with the secular side of life, we can get an inkling into the nature of the society of those times. Social life was permeated by spiritual चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. But people strongly believed in samanvaya or harmonizing the life of this world with the one in the next. सत्य (truth) and धर्म (righteousness) are extolled and अमृतत्व (immortality) as the goal of life accepted. वर्ण system had already taken roots. Monogamy, पोल्य्गम्य् and स्वयṁवर system (that of a bride choosing her husband)—all existed side by side. Agriculture and animal husbandry were the chief means of livelihood. Equitable distribution of wealth was advocated. Civilization was well-developed and fine arts encouraged. Priests and kings were powerful. System of sacrifices had evolved to a high degree of perfection.
Hindu tradition strongly advocates a knowledge of the ṛṣi, the devatā and the छन्दस् of any मन्त्र before using it in the religious rites. Then only will it be effective. Ṛṣi is the sage to whom the मन्त्र was revealed; devatā is the deity to whom the मन्त्र is addressed; and छन्दस् is the metre in which it is composed. According to one calculation the number of ṛṣis exceeds 800 whereas the number of chandases is 19 including the minor variations.
The ब्राह्मणस्, आरण्यकस् and the उपनिषद्स् of this Veda are:
Aitareya and Kauṣītaki ब्राह्मणस्;
Aitareya and Śāṅkhāyana आरण्यकस्; and,
Aitareya and Kauṣītaki Upaniṣads.
Yajurveda Saṁhitā
It is a collection of yajus, the mantras in prose which are specially useful to the अध्वर्यु-priest in the performance of sacrifices.
The Yajurveda Saṁhitā is in two major forms: the Kṛṣṇa and the Śukla, meaning the Black and the White. It is not easy to explain why these two major branches got these names. Though a Saṁhitā (and hence should have been purely in poetry) the former is a mixture of prose and poetry and hence not pure. So, it has been called कृष्ण, the Black one. In contrast, the latter being entirely in poetry, is Śukla, the White one. This is the first explanation. Being more ancient, the former is rather difficult to comprehend and so is कृष्ण or Black. The latter is of more recent origin and hence easier to grasp. So it is Śukla, the White one. This is the second explanation.
Though the Kṛṣṇa यजुर्वेद Saṁhitā is reputed to have had 85 शाखास् or recensions, only four are available now:
Taittirīya;
Maitrāyaṇīya;
Kaṭha;
Kapisthala.
The Taittirīya Saṁhitā which is widely prevalent in South India, has 7 kānḍas or books, 44 prapāṭhakas or chapters, and 651 anuvākas or mantras. It deals mainly with the detailed descriptions of sacrifices like Pauroḍāśa, Yājamāna, वाजपेय, राजसूय, Darśa-pūrṇamāsa and Somayāgas.
The other three शाखास् are not so well-known though they too deal with similar sacrifices. The last of these, the Kapisthala, as available now, seems to be incomplete.
Associated with the Taittirīya Saṁhitā are the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka and the Taittirīya Upaniṣad. The well-known Kaṭhopaniṣad also belongs to Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, but to the Kaṭha recension.
The Śukla यजुर्वेद Saṁhitā, also known as the Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā, is said to have been collected and edited by the famous sage याज्ञवल्क्य. It is entirely in verse and resembles the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā in form. However, there are no sūktas in this. Though 17 शाखास् of this Saṁhitā are said to have existed, only two—the Kāṇva and the Mādhyandina—are available now. The former, more prevalent in the South, has 40 adhyāyas or chapters, 328 anuvākas or sections, and 2,086 mantras. The latter, more common in the North, has 40 adhyāyas, 328 anuvākas, and 1,975 mantras.
Like the Taittirīya Saṁhitā, this Saṁhitā also deals mainly with sacrifices like अग्निष्टोम, वाजपेय and राजसूय.
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, the biggest of the ब्राह्मणस्, and the Bṛhadā-raṇyaka are the ब्राह्मण and the Āraṇyaka attached to the Śukla Yajurveda. Īśāvāsyopaniṣad and Bṛhadāraṇya-kopaniṣad are the उपनिषद्स् of this Veda.
Sāmaveda Saṁhitā
The Sāmaveda Saṁhitā has been highly extolled in our holy books. However, it is not considered as an independent work. ‘Sā’ means ṛk, a मन्त्र of the Ṛgveda. ‘Ama’ means various kinds of musical notes. Hence a ‘sāman’ is a मन्त्र of the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā set to मुसिच्. All such mantras of the Ṛgveda which are useful to the उद्गातृ-priest, have been brought together in this work.
Though it is said to have 1,000 शाखास्, only three are available now: Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya and Jaiminīya.
This Veda is divided into two parts: Ārcikā and Uttarārcikā. The former contains 585 mantras and the latter 964, making a total 1,549. Out of these, except 75 mantras, the rest are taken from the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā. As many as 272 mantras have been repeated twice. If these repetitions are also taken into account, then the number of mantras becomes 1,821. Another recension puts it at 1,875.
Unlike the mantras of the other three वेदस्, the mantras of the Sāmaveda, known simply as sāmans, have seven svaras or musical scales, identical with the seven scales of classical मुसिच्. It can thus be inferred that the origin of Indian classical मुसिच् lies in the Sāmaveda.
There are several varieties of singing the sāmans and they are given special names like Rathantara-sāma, Bṛhat-sāma and so on. It is a difficult art to learn and needs expert guidance.
Nine ब्राह्मणस् are attached to this Veda. Tāṇḍya-mahā-brāhmaṇa is the biggest and the most important of them.
Only one Āraṇyaka of this Veda is available now: Talavakāra or Jaiminīya Āraṇyaka.
Two well-known उपनिषद्स्, the Chāndogya and the Kena (also called Talavakāropaniṣad) are also attached to the Sāmaveda.
Atharvaveda Saṁhitā
Also known as Brahmaveda, since it is assigned to the ब्रह्मा-priest, the Atharvaveda Saṁhitā has some special features because of which it stands apart from the other three वेदस्, specially from the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā. It deals more with the things here and now, than the hereafter, and with the sacrifices which are a means to them. A major part of this Veda is concerned with diseases and their cure, rites for prolonging life, rites for fulfilling one’s desires, building construction, trade and commerce, statecraft, penances and propitiatory rites, as also black magic, though high philosophical ideas much nearer to those of the उपनिषद्स् are also found. Even the literary style is more sophisticated. Hence it is that some scholars believe that this work is chronologically of a later origin and was admitted into the comity of Vedic literature at a later date.
From the ancient times, nine शाखास् of this Veda are known to have existed, but only two are extant: Pippalāda and Śaunaka. It is only the latter that is available in a complete form.
The Atharvaveda Saṁhitā is divided into four prapāṭhakas or books, comprising 20 kāṇḍas or chapters. Each kāṇḍa is divided into sūktas or hymns, and the sūktas into mantras. There are 6,077 mantras, in 736 sūktas spread over 20 kāṇḍas in four prapāṭhakas. The last kāṇḍa, i.e., the 20th, has borrowed heavily from the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā.
This Veda designates God the Absolute not only as ब्रह्मन् but also by some interesting names like स्कम्भ, उच्छिष्ट and Vrātya which are peculiar only to it. The whole universe has emerged out of Him due to His will and is established in Him. He is the Lord of the whole च्रेअतिओन्. The sun, called ‘Rohita’ (the ‘Red One’) is a symbol of His power. And He is the indwelling spirit of human beings also. Those who realize this, go beyond all fear. This Veda also refers to हेअवेन् and हेल्ल्, as also virtue and sin. The qualities like सत्य (truth), दीक्षा (discipline) and तपस् (austerity) that help man to attain perfection are also mentioned.
This work gives us an interesting picture of the society of its times. The land in which the people lived extended from गान्धार (Afghanistan) to Magadha (Bihar) and Vaṅga (Bengal). The वर्ण system had been well-established. The first three varṇas were powerful. Trade and commerce were prosperous though agriculture was the mainstay of the people. Sometimes the ब्राह्मणस् were harassed by the powerful क्षत्त्रिय kings. The cow was highly venerated and गोदान (gift of a cow) was considered meritorious. The institution of मर्रिअगे was similar to that in the Ṛgvedic times.
No Āraṇyaka of the Atharvaveda has come to light so far. Only one ब्राह्मण, the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, has been dis-covered. The three well-known Upaniṣads—the Praśna, the Muṇḍaka and the Māṇḍūkya—belong to this Veda.
Epilogue
As already stated, the Vedic Saṁhitās had to be committed to memory and were passed on orally from generation to generation. Even now they have been preserved in a pure form. This was possible only due to the unique system of chanting that had been evolved, consisting of pada-pāṭha, krama-pāṭha, जटा-pāṭha, and ghana-pāṭha, which are all various chanting modes. (See GHANAPĀṬHA for details)
The वेदस्, considered ‘apauruṣeya’ (not man-made but revealed), are rather difficult to understand due to the archaic form of language and terminology. Hence, the six वेदाङ्गस् (limbs of Veda)—subsidiary sciences that help unfold the Vedic wisdom—came into existence. They are: Śīkṣā, व्याकरण, छन्दस्, निरुक्त, Jyotiṣa and कल्प. Śīkṣā deals with the modes of chanting. व्याकरण is Vedic grammar. छन्दस् is concerned with the details of the metres of Vedic poetry. निरुक्त gives the meanings and explanations of Vedic words. Jyotiṣa, though a work of अस्त्रोनोम्य्, is more directly concerned with the times and periods suitable for the performance of the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. कल्प, in the form of sūtras or aphorisms, has four branches śrauta, gṛhya, धर्म and śulba. It deals with all aspects of sacrificial rites and smaller religious rites performed at home.
In understanding the Vedic literature, bhāṣyas or commentaries have done yeomen service. There have been a galaxy of commentators over the centuries, among whom Sāyaṇācārya (14th cent.) holds a unique place, not only because of the sheer volume of work but also because of the quality. Mention may also be made of some of the other commentators: स्कन्द-svāmin (7th century A. D.); Veṅkaṭa-mādhava (11th century A. D.); भट्ट-भास्कर (11th century A. D.) and आनन्द-तीर्थ (Madhvācārya) (13th cent. A. D.). However, their bhāṣyas as available now are incomplete.
A study of the वेदस् is a fascinating and highly rewarding experience.

vedavratas
------------------------------------------
Brahmacārins residing in the गुरु-kulas for learning the वेदस् had to observe some vratas or religious vows before commencing the study of certain sections of the same. They were enumerated as four: Mahānāmnīvrata; महाव्रत; Upaniṣadvrata; Godānavrata.
They were each of one year’s duration, starting from the age 13, up to the age of 16.
However, they seem to have been given up in course of time.

Vedavatī
------------------------------------------
Vedavatī was the daughter of the sage Kuśadhvaja. She was extraordinarily beautiful. When she was doing tapas—severe austerities—to get Lord विष्णु as her husband, रावण tried to molest her. She escaped from him, cursed him that she will get him killed in her next birth, and immolated herself in the Vedic fire. She was later born as सीता (Rāmāyaṇa, Uttarakāṇḍa, Chapter 17), the foster daughter of जनक.

Vedānta Deśika
(A.

-1137), वेदान्त देशिक was the chief architect who established the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta on a firm foundation and shaped the श्रीवैष्णव cult into a well-knit movement.
He was born at काञ्चीपुरम् (in Tamil Nadu) as the only son of Anantasūri and Totāramma by the grace of Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara of तिरुपति. Hence he was named Veṅkaṭanātha.
He had an excellent एदुचतिओन् under his uncle, आत्रेय Rāmānuja and became an erudite scholar even by the age of twenty one.
He was married to Tirumaṅgai who proved to be an ideal wife, fully co-operating with the husband in his spiritual aspirations.
Throughout his life वेदान्त देशिक worked hard and vigorously to propagate Rāmānuja’s philosophy and religion (Śrīvaiṣṇavism) through discourses, disputations with other schools and writing books. He was a prolific writer, whose writings exceed a hundred treatises and compositions.
He toured the country extensively especially visiting the places connected with वैष्णविस्म्.
He was the आचार्य of the pontifical seat at काञ्चीपुरम्, one of the 74 established by Rāmānuja.
His very goodness and greatness created enemies for him as it has happened in the case of many a great man. However, by the very dint of that greatness he could vanquish them all.
Apart from his erudition in the scriptures, he was also a great poet and dramatist. He had perfect command over the Tamil language also and had mastered the Prabandham literature of the आऌवार्स्.
The following are a few of his more well-known works:
Arthapañcaka; Dayāśataka; Dramiḍopaniṣatsāra; Haṁsasandeśa;Īśopaniṣadbhāṣya; Pādukāsahasra;Rahasyatrayasāra; Saṅkalpasūryodaya;Śatadūṣaṇī; Subhāṣitanīvī; Tātparyacandrikā; Tattvamuktākalāpa.
His son Varadanātha proved worthy of the ड़थेर् by his life and scholarship.
The परकाल मठ, one of the important monasteries of the श्रीवैष्णव school, was established by Brahmatantra Svatantra Jīyar (A.

-1386), a saṁnyāsin disciple of वेदान्त देशिक, under his inspiration.
See also ŚRĪVAIṢṆAVISM.

Vedārambha
(‘beginning [the first study] of the वेदस्’)
------------------------------------------
In the most ancient days, the study of the वेदस् commenced just after the उपनयन ceremony. However, as the study of the वेदस् was relegated to the background due to the rise of the non-Vedic literature and its study, a new saṁskāra or sacrament called वेदारम्भ was introduced after उपनयन and before समावर्तन (See UPANAYANA and SAMĀVARTANA for details.). This was to be done if the ब्रह्मचारिन् wished to study the वेदस् also.
This simple ceremony consisted of the following steps: Ābhyudayikaśrāddha or Nāndīśrāddha; establishing the laukikāgni (domestic fire); offerings of ghee into the fire; gifts to the officiating ब्राह्मण.
The pattern of offerings was as follows:
To begin the study of Deity
Ṛgveda Bhū (earth) and Agni
Yajurveda Antarikṣa (space) and Vāyu
Sāmaveda Dyaus (heaven) and सूर्य or Āditya
Atharvaveda Diśaḥ (quarters) and चन्द्र or Soma

Two offerings of ghee were made to the deities.
This was followed by होम (domestic fire ritual) to ब्रह्मन्, छन्दस् and प्रजापति as also दक्षिणा (fees) and दान (gifts) to the officiating priest.
Then commenced the teaching of the Veda.

Vedic Sacrifices
------------------------------------------
Introduction
In Indian vernaculars, especially those derived from Sanskrit, the word ‘yajña’ is commonly used to indicate any work that involves great effort and needs the active co-operation of many. It is perhaps an indication of the tremendous inﬂuence the system of Vedic sacrifices— generally called as yajñas or yāgas— has had on the Hindu society over the millennia.
Fortunately for the scholars of Indology and Vedic studies, वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् have not totally disappeared as yet, though they have become very rare. Even during this 20th century, as many as 70 वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् are known to have been performed. They include the well-known sacrifices like अग्निष्टोम, अप्तोर्याम, अतिरात्र, चातुर्मास्य, निरूढपशुबन्ध, सौत्रामणी and वाजपेय.
Āhitāgnis (those who have ceremonially established the Vedic fires) are to be found even today. However they seem to be slowly becoming a vanishing species.
By the time of the Ṛgvedasaṁhitā itself, considered to be the oldest among the Vedas—nay, the oldest scripture in the world—Vedic sacrificial system seems to have taken a definite and clear shape. Names of the Vedic fires like the गार्हपत्य, of some sacrifices like the अतिरात्र, of the sixteen priests needed in a सोमयाग like होतृ, neṣṭṛ and आग्नीध्र, of the implements used like यूप (sacrificial post), जुहू (wooden ladle) and चमस (wooden vessel for the सोम juice), as also some technical terms like आहाव (call, seeking permission, by the होतृ priest) and अवभृथ (concluding bath) find a place in the Ṛgvedic hymns, thereby confirming the inference drawn above.
A study of the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् helps in a proper understanding of the Vedic literature as such, since the latter is closely connected with the former. In fact, the very arrangement of the mantras in the Vedic Saṁhitās to suit the sacrificial needs, supports this view. Hence such a study can be useful in fixing the chronology of the Vedic literature, the development and stratification of the different portions of that literature and the inﬂuence that literature has exerted on the वर्ण-system and the caste-system.
Basic Literature
Information about the sacrifices has been spread out, all over the Vedic literature. In the ब्राह्मणस् one can get more details including instructions for their performance. However, it is in the श्रौतसूत्रस् and the शुल्बसूत्रस् that a systematic treatment of the subject is obtained. Whereas the latter is concerned solely with the constructional and engineering aspects of a sacrifice like the measurement and formation of the वेदि (altar), it is the former that is the functional manual for the priests and hence gives us the modus operandi of the various rites in detail. Therefore its help is invaluable in the study of Vedic rituals.
